newsitem.title: USA: Government should not decide paternal leave - Dole.
newsitem.headline: Government should not decide paternal leave - Dole.

text.p: Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole on Saturday criticised a federal law letting workers take time off to care for a new baby or sick family member, as he preached a message of lower taxes and less government in this key state.

Meeting small business people in a "listening to America" event at a tennis equipment company, Dole said he had compassion for families, but called the Family and Medical Leave law unneeded government intrusion.

President Bill Clinton, who signed the measure early in his term, has called it one of his proudest achievements and plans to send legislation to Congress to expand the act as well as allow workers to trade overtime for compensatory time to meet family obligations.
Eager to court women voters, Democrats highlighted the law and other "pro-family" initiatives during their national convention in Chicago. Dole has had trouble attracting female voters.

"My view is why should the federal government be getting into family leave? It ought to be left to the employees or the state or the county and the federal government ought to be out of it," Dole said.
"I believe in compassionate leave if there is a birth or a death or there is something that happens in a family ... but I again wonder about the long arm of the government," he said.
Dole later issued a statement saying he supported an initiative to give workers more flexibility to use their comp time, a separate issue from family leave.

The family leave law allows most workers 12 weeks of unpaid leave a year for family illness, adoption or childbirth. Clinton wants to expand the law to allow workers more time off for family emergencies, but a White House spokesman said it was unlikely the law would pass this year.

"Now once again (Dole's) resisting an idea that's helped 12 million Americans deal with family problems and keep their jobs. Resisting new ideas is no way to move into the 21st century," said Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart.

At a rally later on Saturday before cheering students at eastern Pennyslvania's University of Scranton, a Jesuit school, Dole criticised Clinton for vetoing legislation to outlaw so-called "partial birth abortions," a rare late-term procedure.

"Whether you're pro-life or pro-choice I think there's one thing most everyone can agree on, partial birth abortion is wrong," Dole said. Congressional Republican leaders will try to override Clinton's veto later this month.
The one-day Pennsylvania trip is Dole's third visit in recent weeks. Polls show him lagging Clinton in this state, which has 23 electoral college votes, making it a key election battleground.

In appearances here on Saturday as well as in his response to Clinton's weekly radio address, Dole showcased his economic plan, which calls for a 15 percent tax cut and halving of the capital gains tax.

Dole promised he can deliver the tax cuts and balance the budget at the same time, without cutting Social Security or Medicare. The White House says Dole's plan will force big cuts in the popular programmes.

Dole faced an unexpected tough question at his "listening to America" session at Gamma Sports Inc. in Pittsburgh, where he sat in a director's chair before towering boxes of tennis equipment for a chat with carefully selected small business people.

Christiane Vaflor, 20, a University of Pittsburgh senior, attempted to ask Dole about Republican plans to reduce direct college student loans, but Dole never directly answered the question. Instead, Pennsylvania Republican Sen. Rick Santorum angrily denied that Republicans cut student aid.

When Vaflor attempted to follow up, Jim Quinn, a local talk radio host, shouted her down saying, "You want to be an entrepeneur and you can't find the resources to fund your own education?" as the audience applauded.
Vaflor later said Dole should have responded, complaining: "I'm putting myself through college, I've worked two jobs every semester."
